title: Settling to reproduce: metabolic, immune, and reproductive trajectories after immigration in female bonobos
abstract: Abstract Dispersal and social integration shape opportunities for cooperation and have played a central role in human evolution. Yet, immigration and settlement often entail costs for dispersers, including elevated risks of injury, mortality, or reproductive suppression. In primates, female immigrants commonly face aggression and social instability during settlement. Bonobos (Pan paniscus) differ in that affiliative integration may mitigate these challenges, but the physiological and reproductive consequences of immigration remain poorly understood. We investigated post-immigration physiological and reproductive trajectories in wild female bonobos using longitudinal measurements of urinary cortisol, triiodothyronine (T3), neopterin, and a progesterone metabolite (PdG) over up to eight years post-immigration. T3 and neopterin levels showed no systematic change with time since immigration. Cortisol levels increased gradually with time, a pattern consistent with developmental maturation. A post-immigration PdG elevation was detected in 13 of 17 females, with 12 detections occurring within two years after immigration. Nine females gave birth at a median of 3.8 years post-immigration. We found no evidence of the predicted pattern of early physiological disturbance followed by recovery. These trajectories suggest an absence of prolonged settlement-related metabolic or immunological disruption and are consistent with the hypothesis that species-typical social tolerance and affiliation may buffer settlement-related challenges.
